title: JD Vance and the VP curse
subtitle: If you’re the VP to an unpopular president, the rest of your career usually doesn’t go well. Plus, a post-midterm Republican primary draft on Still Counting EP12.
contentHtml:
We’re back to our regular schedule for Still Counting after taping bonus episodes last week and this weekend.1 So this is our regular Wednesday episode. After considering how the extraordinary midterm landslide might affect Democrats’ 2028 plans, we turned to Republicans this time.

Audio version here. Your reviews, comments, likes and subscribes are always appreciated.

The context

I won’t speak for Galen and Clare, but I found drafting the Republicans less fun than the Democrats. That’s partly because the field is top-heavy. The top three Republican contenders, deemed by prediction markets to be JD Vance, Marco Rubio and Ron DeSantis, together have about a two-thirds chance of being the nominee, leaving little win probability for anyone else.

You could argue that’s miscalibrated, though for better or worse, it roughly tracks polls — which are more predictive than you might assume even at this stage — where Vance and Rubio are way ahead of anyone else, including DeSantis.

But Vance’s odds have plummeted since Labor Day, when Democrats began to surge in midterm polls. I don’t think prediction market traders get everything right, but the notion that a bad midterm result for Trump might encourage voters to look beyond the vice president for a successor seems sound enough.

JD Vance's odds have plummeted since Labor Day

DeSantis has been the biggest recent riser, meanwhile. I guess the thinking here is that he’s still MAGA-y enough to get away with criticizing Republicans while offering some degree of proven electoral performance and not being directly tied to the deeply unpopular administration. His poor performance in the 2024 nomination race raises the question of whether his 2022 popularity surge was an artifact of COVID plus the fact that Florida has now become really red. Overall, though, the field has opened up, with Vance and Rubio going from a 70 percent combined chance of being the nominee to just under 50 percent now.

But I’m not here to talk about DeSantis or the rest of the field. Instead, let’s consider the vice president, whom we’ve sparsely covered at Silver Bulletin. Vance issued his own election post-mortem, which placed almost all of the blame directly or indirectly on the Iran War, where he’s made his disagreements with Trump known through frequent leaks to the press.

Some conservatives have started to question whether Vance should even run in 2028. Unlike the Democratic nomination, the GOP nod in two years is perhaps not all that desirable. Unless President Trump’s dismal approval ratings improve, the election figures to be an uphill battle for Republicans. Meanwhile, the filtering effect of having to implicitly or explicitly receive Trump’s seal of approval has squashed intellectual diversity in the party. You can name the exceptions — successful non-MAGA Republicans, like Brian Kemp in Georgia, Kelly Ayotte in New Hampshire, and Spencer Cox in Utah — on one hand. And most of them probably aren’t prominent enough or conservative enough to make a serious bid.2

Trump’s situation could improve. Recent political history is full of examples where the conventional wisdom over-extrapolated from the results of a single election. Trump himself has made big comebacks too, returning to the presidency four years after being impeached for the second time. Gas prices might decline, the war might end, and Democrats have nominated a series of C-tier presidential nominees lately.

But consider the headlines from this week:

  • Republicans had to fend off an impeachment attempt against Pete Hegseth led by the outgoing Republican congressman Thomas Massie;

  • An interest-rate hike has become highly likely after a hot inflation report;

  • Nvidia CEO and Trump ally Jensen Huang stepped down after acknowledging infidelity amid reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The New York Times also reported an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him.

  • Trump replaced Susie Wiles as chief of staff with Stephen Miller, who is associated with the hardline immigration policies that even the most moderate Democrats successfully campaigned against last week.

  • And Scott Colom was declared the winner in Mississippi.

Plus, Trump is 80 years old, the point at which visible signs of Joe Biden’s age-related decline really started to accelerate. Meanwhile, Republicans have consistently struggled to win elections during the Trump Era when Trump himself wasn’t on the ballot, and he’s notorious for not really caring much about the fate of other Republicans.

Could Vance succeed at distancing himself from Trump on Iran or other issues? Disagreements between the president and the vice president were common until recently. Before the passage of the 12th Amendment in 1804, a rivalry was unavoidable because the second-place finisher in the presidential race became the vice president. (Imagine if Kamala Harris were still VP today, but under Trump.) In 1832, John Calhoun actually resigned the vice presidency because of his differences with Andrew Jackson. One of FDR’s vice presidents, John Nance Garner, ran against him for the 1940 nomination. LBJ bitterly feuded with the Kennedys (mostly Bobby). And more recently, rioters at the Capitol during the Jan. 6 insurrection chanted “Hang Mike Pence” after Pence refused to interrupt the certification of Biden’s win in 2020.

The modern level of high partisan loyalty makes it harder for vice presidents to distance themselves from their boss’s policies, however. Harris completely failed to differentiate herself from Biden, and didn’t even try. Trump’s tendency to punish dissent puts Vance in a box, meanwhile.

Nor had Vance particularly been a strong electoral performer. Prior to winning the vice presidency, his only previous bid for office came in 2022, when he won Ohio’s Senate race by 6 points but underperformed Ohio’s Republican governor, Mike DeWine, who won re-election by 25 points instead.

There’s also another unfavorable trend for Vance. In recent years, while vice presidents to unpopular presidents have frequently won their party’s nominations, they’ve developed a poor track record in general elections. There basically isn’t any good example since presidential approval ratings began of the VP to an unpopular president later being elected president himself.

Let’s run back the tape to the mid-1960s, considering every vice president since Humphrey. I figure this is the relevant dataset because it coincides with the development of the modern presidential nomination system, which emerged over roughly 1968-1980 and gave voters more say in the process.

Hubert H. Humphrey (1965-1969 under Lyndon Baines Johnson)

LBJ was initially on track to seek a second elected term, but bowed out after only getting 49.6 percent of the vote, as a write-in candidate, against Eugene McCarthy in the New Hampshire primary, a watershed moment for popular participation mattering in the nomination process. However, Humphrey eventually received the nomination over the anti-war McCarthy at the Democrats’ infamous and violent 1968 convention in Chicago. Despite the problems in Chicago, Humphrey only barely lost the popular vote to Richard Nixon, but Nixon’s Electoral College margin was sound (the populist, segregationist George Wallace received 46 electoral votes). Humphrey sought the 1972 nomination, but lost to the left-wing George McGovern, who benefited from having helped to design the rules of the new nomination system.

Spiro Agnew (1969-1973 under Richard Nixon)

Agnew resigned the vice presidency amid a bribery scandal unrelated to Watergate nine months into Nixon’s second term and never ran for office again.

Gerald Ford (1973-1974 under Richard Nixon)

Ford ascended to the presidency after Nixon’s resignation and won a highly contentious 1976 nomination as an unelected incumbent against Ronald Reagan. But Ford lost the November election to Jimmy Carter. (Although as with Humphrey in 1968, it was closer than you might expect under the circumstances.) Ford did not appear on an election ballot again, but made a play to be Reagan’s running mate at the GOP convention in 1980.

Nelson Rockefeller (1974-1977 under Gerald Ford)

After a fairly distinguished career with four terms as governor of New York, Rockefeller was 68 years old at the time his vice presidency tenure ended and his moderation was out of step with the Reagan Revolution. He died two years later.

Walter Mondale (1977-1981 under Jimmy Carter)

Mondale won the Democratic nomination in 1984 in a contentious race against Gary Hart and Jesse Jackson, and then lost in a landslide to Reagan. So this is one of the better examples of it being hard to escape the shadow of an unpopular president, even if you wait four years to run yourself. Mondale became Paul Wellstone’s replacement in the 2002 Minnesota Senate race after Wellstone died in a plane crash, but lost by 2 points to Norm Coleman.

George H.W. Bush (1981-1989 under Ronald Reagan)

Bush Sr. claimed the 1988 GOP nomination after an initial stumble in Iowa and was elected easily over Michael Dukakis — though Dukakis had led for parts of the race — producing a third consecutive Republican term. His popularity skyrocketed after the Gulf War but plummeted just as the economy struggled to recover from a recession and high inflation. He faced growing strains of populism — Pat Buchanan within the Republican Party, Ross Perot — before losing to Bill Clinton in an election in which he got only 37.5 percent of the popular vote.

Dan Quayle (1989-1993 under George H.W. Bush)

Always considered a lightweight, Quayle skipped the 1996 race and made an all-in play for Iowa during the 2000 Republican nomination, where he was running against Bush Jr., but withdrew in September 1999 after making no traction in the polls.

Al Gore (1993-2001 under Bill Clinton)

Gore swept all 50 states in winning the 2000 nomination over Bill Bradley, but lost the Electoral College to Bush Jr. by 537 votes following a recount in Florida (that was halted by the Supreme Court). He remained a reasonably prominent public figure for some time, focusing on the environment, but hasn’t sought public office again.

Dick Cheney (2001-2009 under George W. Bush)

Never considered to have presidential ambitions on his own, Cheney didn’t run in 2008, depriving us of a data point from one of the better precedents for Trump’s second term.

Joe Biden (2009-2017 under Barack Obama)

Chosen by Obama in part because Obama considered him too old to run for president himself3, Biden seriously considered running in 2016 but ceded to Hillary Clinton. He did seek the 2020 nomination at age 76, where he was treated as an underdog by many pundits despite always polling strongly, then boomeranged to win after strong showings in South Carolina and on Super Tuesday. The nomination race that year was one of the clearest examples of a party putting a finger on the scale, with a series of endorsements for Biden as trepidation about a Bernie Sanders nomination and the COVID pandemic motivated the party to rally behind the perceived safer choice. Biden defeated Trump that November, though in an election that was closer than polls projected.

Buoyed by a comparatively strong showing by Democrats in the 2022 midterm, Biden sought a second term when many Democrats assumed he wouldn’t. Amid supermajorities of voters expressing concerns about his age, he fared disastrously at a June 2024 debate against Trump, and eventually stood down after a power struggle, while making it clear that Harris was his second choice.

Mike Pence (2017-2021 under Donald Trump)

A fairly conventional vice president in one of Trump’s more orthodox campaign decisions, Pence refused to prevent the certification of the 2020 presidential vote under pressure from Trump and protesters at the Jan. 6 insurrection. He sought the 2024 nomination but rarely escaped the single digits in polls. Pence refused to endorse Trump in the November general election.

Kamala Harris (2021-2025 under Joe Biden)

Chosen by Biden as his running mate in 2020 despite flopping in the Democratic nomination race and exiting early, in part because of identity politics dynamics within the party, Harris was given a challenging portfolio by Biden in a way that possibly undermined her ability to develop star power of her own and become the logical “bridge” after a caretaker term. Replacing Biden in July 2024 after 25 days of intensive drama, Harris hit the ground running and initially gained momentum amid Brat Summer, but was unable or unwilling to sufficiently distance herself from Biden and had trouble defining a clear brand or lane for herself. She lost to Trump in November in an election that was closer than the mandate it was sometimes interpreted as being. Still, she was the first Democrat since 2004 to lose the popular vote and underperformed Democratic Senate candidates in key states. She is reportedly considering running again in 2028.

JD Vance (2025- under Donald Trump)

So this starts to look like a pretty bad track record for Vance.

Which other vice presidents sought the presidency after serving under presidents who were unpopular near the end of their presidencies4? Bush, Biden and Gore don’t count because Reagan, Obama and Clinton were reasonably popular as of the end of their terms.5

Humphrey lost. Ford lost. Mondale lost in a landslide. Quayle and Pence had no hope of winning their nominations. Harris lost, narrowly.

Among the VPs to relatively popular presidents, Gore lost too. Biden won after a four-year hiatus but is likely to be remembered by history as having held on too long in seeking a second term. H.W. Bush is the clearest success story but, like Biden, was a one-termer.

Sure, a couple of those elections — Gore’s certainly — might have gone the other way. But in recent years, we’ve added Harris and Pence as failures. And if you ask me, Biden looks like a cautionary tale too.

Maybe this is a case of just not enough data to make for reliable extrapolations. We’re talking about nine examples here, not dozens. And some of them are only partial failures.

And as I said, VPs have good track records of winning party nominations; it’s general elections that have been the trouble spot.

But that may partly reflect power vacuums within their parties. Just like someone has to be the Minnesota Vikings’ quarterback, someone has to win the Republican nomination in two years.

But parties with lame-duck presidents are often stuck between a rock and a hard place. The existing president is term-limited — or too old or unpopular to run again. Meanwhile, he’ll often have squashed or discredited opposition in his party. And presidents usually have poor midterms that deprive the party of fresh prospects. So the bill comes due, and the honor of paying it often defaults to the veep. But it’s not the sort of check that candidates are necessarily lining up to pay.

2

Or in the case of Florida Governor-elect Byron Donalds, my 3rd-round pick, they’re too new in office. There’s no constitutional problem for Donalds, but candidates rarely immediately turn around and run for president after winning a major statewide office for the first time. (I’m not sure whether I’d classify Donalds as MAGA.)

3

Though I’ll note that the reporting on this claim is a bit speculative; there’s no definitive account of it.

4

This phrasing is intentional; presidents sometimes get a sort of sympathy/reverse-honeymoon approval rating bounce toward the very end of their terms once their parties have lost the election or are transitioning out of power.

5

Although to varying degrees, they experienced approval-rating slumps in the middle of their terms.
